title: Isaiah 45:1–13
context: After 44:21–28—Remember these things, O Jacob, servant formed and not forgotten; transgressions blotted like a cloud; heavens singing because the LORD has redeemed Jacob; Cyrus named my shepherd who shall fulfill all my purpose; Jerusalem built and the temple’s foundation laid—the word turns: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, belts of kings loosed and gates opened, treasures of darkness, called by name though he does not know me, I am the LORD and there is no other, I form light and create darkness, shower O heavens righteousness, woe to him who strives with his Maker, and Cyrus stirred in righteousness to build my city and set the exiles free—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 45:1–13.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: His anointed—His king, whom God has designed, and separated, and fitted, in all respects, for this work. Loose—I will take away their girdle, which was about their loins; their power and authority, whereof that was an ensign. Gates—The great and magnificent gates of their cities and palaces, which shall be opened to him as conqueror. Go—To remove all obstructions, to destroy all them that oppose thee, and carry thee through the greatest difficulties. The treasures—Such as have been long kept in dark and secret places. I have—I knew, and called thee by thy name, when thou didst neither know nor think of me; nay, when thou hadst no being. I girded—I made thee strong and active, and disposed thee for these great and warlike enterprizes. That—That all nations may know it by my foretelling these things so long before, and by the wonderful success that I shall give thee, and by my over-ruling thine heart and counsels, to the deliverance of my people. Light—All mens comforts and calamities come from thy hand. Drop—The righteous and gracious acts of God for his people, shall be so many, as if God rained showers of righteousness out of heaven. It—This great work of salvation and righteousness; whereof, tho’ Cyrus is the instrument, I am the author. Woe—As God here makes many glorious promises to Cyrus, so he pronounces a curse upon them, who should endeavour to hinder him. Contend—Contend, if you please, with your fellow creatures, but not with your creator. Thus saith—Will you not allow me that liberty which yourselves take, of disposing of my own children and works, as I see fit? Him—Cyrus. In righteousness—Most justly, to punish the wicked Babylonians, to plead the cause of the oppressed ones, to manifest my righteousness, and truth, and goodness.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 45:1–13)

reformed.quote: Pursues the subject. Names the person by whose hand he will bring them back. Calls Cyrus his Anointed: designation of Israel’s and Judah’s kings representing Christ; bestowed on a heathen king not by a perpetual title, but because he discharged for a time the office of Redeemer—avenged and delivered the Church from the Assyrians. Instructed by Daniel; regarded the God of Israel with reverence as Highest, but was not converted and did not forsake superstitions. For this single benefit (the Church’s salvation) a heathen is called the Messiah/Anointed. Historic Persian Cyrus, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9. Loose the loins of kings: deprived of strength and authority. Gates cannot resist God. Easy rapid victory; God removes obstructions. Treasures of darkness: hidden; historically Croesus of Lydia. That thou mayest know I am Jehovah: special knowledge for the work, not regeneration. Call by name = chosen for a particular work (cf. Isa 43:1), not the flock-calling of believers (John 10:3). For Jacob my servant’s sake and Israel mine elect: free-grace election; they do not make themselves servants. Cyrus has not known me: not his merits. I am Jehovah; I have girded thee though thou hast not known me; he presides over wars. All nations shall know—not necessarily immediately; the return is prelude to future redemption. Forming light / creating darkness: peace and war, prosperous and adverse. Fanatics who make God the author of sin (guilt) abuse the passage. God is author of the evil of punishment, not of the evil of guilt; he uses wicked men to chastise (Pharaoh) without inspiring their malice. Commands heaven and earth to bring forth salvation and righteousness. First: deliverance from Babylon, Cyrus the instrument. Then a spiritual import to the kingdom of Christ, but first the simple interpretation about the return from captivity. Woe restrains murmurers who in adversity strive with God. Isaiah reasons about the course of the present life; Paul in Rom 9 ascends to heavenly and eternal life. Do not prescribe to God how to treat his sons and works. I have raised him up in righteousness: Him is Cyrus; he shall build my city (by edicts, Ezra/2 Chr) and release captives not for a price.

verses.text: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed:
verses.arminianNotes:
Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed. Wesley: His anointed—His king, whom God has designed, and separated, and fitted, in all respects, for this work. Loose—I will take away their girdle, which was about their loins; their power and authority, whereof that was an ensign. Gates—The great and magnificent gates of their cities and palaces, which shall be opened to him as conqueror.

Arminian hearing: anointed is his king, designed, separated, and fitted for this work; belts loosed are girdle, power, and authority taken; gates of cities and palaces open to the conqueror. Shared loudly with Calvin: historic Persian Cyrus, the LORD’s anointed for this work, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9. Historic Cyrus, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “His anointed—His king” and “Loose—girdle about their loins” are his lemmas for ESV “his anointed” and “loose the belts of kings,” not a different verse. No open theism: designed and fitted already; the right hand is grasped. Prefer no keyContrast on 1: both camps take historic Cyrus as anointed for this work; do not invent a millennial or two-anointeds fight. Match 44:28: Cyrus my shepherd, temple foundation laid. Match v. 13: the same him stirred in righteousness to build the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus. Calvin: pursues 44’s subject; names the person by whose hand he will bring them back; turns to Cyrus himself. Calls Cyrus his Anointed: the designation of Israel’s and Judah’s kings representing Christ, bestowed on a heathen king not by a perpetual title, but because he discharged for a time the office of Redeemer—avenged and delivered the Church from the Assyrians. Instructed by Daniel; regarded the God of Israel with reverence as Highest, but was not converted and did not forsake superstitions. For this single benefit (the Church’s salvation) a heathen is called the Messiah/Anointed. Loose the loins of kings: deprived of strength and authority. Gates cannot resist God.

Reformed hearing: Anointed is a time-bound Redeemer-office for the Church’s deliverance, not conversion and not a perpetual messianic title. Shared loudly with Wesley: historic Persian Cyrus, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9. Historic Cyrus, not a newspaper, not a living politician, not a millennial fork. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Anointed/Meschiae” and “loose the loins of kings” are his lemmas for ESV “his anointed” and “loose the belts of kings.” Prefer no keyContrast on 1: both camps shout the same historic Cyrus; do not invent two anointeds. Match 44:28: shepherd who shall fulfill all my purpose. Match v. 13: him who builds the city and sets the exiles free.

verses.text: “I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron,
verses.arminianNotes:
I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron. Wesley: Go—To remove all obstructions, to destroy all them that oppose thee, and carry thee through the greatest difficulties.

Arminian hearing: the LORD goes before to remove obstructions, destroy opposers, and carry Cyrus through the greatest difficulties. Shared: I will go before you; bronze doors broken; iron bars cut. Historic Persian campaign, not a newspaper war. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Go” is his lemma for “I will go before you.” Prefer no keyContrast: both camps hear easy victory by the LORD’s going before. Match v. 1: gates opened to the conqueror. Match v. 3: treasures wait behind those doors.
verses.reformedNotes:
I will go before you and level the exalted places. Calvin: easy, rapid victory; God removes obstructions. Doors of bronze broken; bars of iron cut through.

Reformed hearing: the LORD levels what is exalted and takes the gates himself; Cyrus’s speed is the LORD’s going before. Shared with Wesley: obstructions removed; bronze and iron give way. Historic Persian victory, not a newspaper, not a millennial chart. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “removes obstructions” names the same going-before as Wesley’s Go. Prefer no keyContrast. Match v. 1: gates cannot resist God. Match v. 3: treasures of darkness given after the bars are cut.

verses.text: I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name.
verses.arminianNotes:
I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name. Wesley: The treasures—Such as have been long kept in dark and secret places.

Arminian hearing: treasures long kept in the dark are given so Cyrus may know it is the LORD, the God of Israel, who calls him by name. Shared: treasures of darkness; hoards in secret places; called by name. Historic hoards, not a newspaper vault. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “The treasures—dark and secret places” is his lemma for “treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places.” No open theism: he calls him by name; the knowing is that it is the LORD who calls. Prefer no keyContrast: skip Calvin’s Croesus and not-regeneration rather than invent a Wesley fight. Match v. 2: bars cut, then hoards given. Match v. 4: called by name for Jacob’s sake, though he does not know me.
verses.reformedNotes:
I will give you the treasures of darkness. Calvin: hidden treasures; historically Croesus of Lydia. That thou mayest know I am Jehovah: special knowledge for the work, not regeneration, not the Spirit of regeneration. Call by name: chosen for a particular work (cf. Isa 43:1), not the flock-calling of believers (John 10:3).

Reformed hearing: Croesus’s hoards as the dark treasures; Cyrus knows Jehovah for this work, not as a converted sheep of John 10. Shared with Wesley: treasures long kept in the dark; called by name. Historic Lydia and Persia, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “That thou mayest know I am Jehovah” is his lemma for “that you may know that it is I, the LORD.” Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley’s thin treasures-lemma does not fight Calvin’s not-regeneration; skip rather than invent. Match v. 4: named though he does not know me. Match v. 5: I equip you, though you do not know me.

verses.text: For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me.
verses.arminianNotes:
For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. Wesley: I have—I knew, and called thee by thy name, when thou didst neither know nor think of me; nay, when thou hadst no being.

Arminian hearing: named for Jacob’s sake when Cyrus neither knew nor thought of the LORD—nay, when he had no being. Shared: for Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen; called by name though he does not know me. Historic Cyrus named before birth, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “I have—I knew, and called thee” is his lemma for “I call you by your name, I name you.” No open theism: he named him when he had no being; he is not discovering whom to call. Prefer no keyContrast: both camps hear named-before-he-knew for Jacob’s sake. Match 44:28: Cyrus named two hundred years before he was born. Match v. 3: who call you by your name. Match v. 5: I equip you, though you do not know me.
verses.reformedNotes:
For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen. Calvin: free-grace election; they do not make themselves servants. Cyrus has not known me: not his merits; he must not despise the Jews. Josephus’s Alexander anecdote is Calvin’s illustration of unusual preservation—not the verse’s referent.

Reformed hearing: Jacob is servant by free-grace election, not self-made; Cyrus is named for their sake, without merit and without knowing him. Shared with Wesley: for Jacob and Israel; named though he does not know me. Historic Cyrus for Jacob’s sake, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Israel mine elect” is his lemma for “Israel my chosen.” No open theism: named before he knew; election already stands. Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley’s when-thou-hadst-no-being and Calvin’s free-grace-for-Jacob overlap as named-before-merit. Match v. 1: anointed Cyrus. Match v. 13: stirred in righteousness for the exiles.

verses.text: I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me,
verses.arminianNotes:
I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me. Wesley: I girded—I made thee strong and active, and disposed thee for these great and warlike enterprizes.

Arminian hearing: he girded Cyrus—made him strong and active and disposed him for warlike enterprizes—though Cyrus does not know him. Shared sovereignty: I am the LORD, and there is no other; besides me there is no God. Historic Cyrus equipped, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “I girded” is his lemma for ESV “I equip you.” No open theism: there is no other; he already equips. Prefer no keyContrast: 45:5–6 are shared sovereignty. Match v. 4: named though he does not know me. Match v. 6: that people may know there is none besides me.
verses.reformedNotes:
I am the LORD, and there is no other. Calvin: I am Jehovah; I have girded thee though thou hast not known me. Courage from the Lord; he presides over wars.

Reformed hearing: Jehovah girds the unknown king; courage and wars are his. Shared with Wesley: I am the LORD and there is no other; girded/equipped though he does not know me. Historic Persian wars under the LORD’s girding, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “I have girded thee” is his lemma for ESV “I equip you.” No open theism: besides me there is no God; he is not becoming God as the campaign unfolds. Prefer no keyContrast: 45:5–6 shared sovereignty. Match v. 4: though you do not know me. Match v. 7: I am the LORD, who does all these things.

verses.text: that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other.
verses.arminianNotes:
that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. Wesley: That—That all nations may know it by my foretelling these things so long before, and by the wonderful success that I shall give thee, and by my over-ruling thine heart and counsels, to the deliverance of my people.

Arminian hearing: nations know by the long-before prediction, by Cyrus’s success, and by the LORD over-ruling his heart and counsels to deliver Israel. Shared sovereignty: from the rising of the sun and from the west, none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. Historic nations and the return, not a newspaper, not a millennial chart. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “That—all nations may know” is his lemma for “that people may know.” No open theism: foretold so long before; heart over-ruled. Prefer no keyContrast: skip Calvin’s “not necessarily immediately” rather than invent a timetable fight. Match v. 5: no other God. Match v. 4: named when he had no being.
verses.reformedNotes:
that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me. Calvin: all nations shall know—not necessarily immediately; the return is prelude to future redemption. Do not millennial-chart this.

Reformed hearing: east and west will know there is none besides him; the return is prelude, not a finished timetable. Shared with Wesley: all nations know; I am the LORD and there is no other. Historic return as prelude, not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “all nations shall know” is his lemma for “that people may know.” Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley’s foretelling-and-success and Calvin’s prelude overlap as the nations’ knowing; do not invent a millennial fork. Match v. 5: no other God. Match v. 8: heavens rain righteousness after this knowing.

verses.text: I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things. Wesley: Light—All mens comforts and calamities come from thy hand.

Arminian hearing: all men’s comforts and calamities come from his hand; he forms light and creates darkness. Shared sovereignty: I form light and create darkness; I am the LORD, who does all these things. Historic Maker of well-being and calamity, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: ESV “well-being and calamity”; Wesley’s KJV lemma is “peace and evil”—comforts and calamities from thy hand, not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast on 7: Wesley’s comforts-and-calamities and Calvin’s punishment-not-guilt overlap; skip thin-versus-thick. No open theism: he does all these things; fortune is not a rival. Match v. 5–6: I am the LORD and there is no other. Match v. 9: the same Maker the clay must not strive with.
verses.reformedNotes:
I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity. Calvin: forming light / creating darkness is peace and war, prosperous and adverse—not only those two. Peace versus evil names afflictions, wars, adverse events. Fanatics who make God the author of sin (guilt) abuse the passage. Ordinary distinction: God is author of the evil of punishment, not of the evil of guilt. He uses wicked men to chastise (Pharaoh) without inspiring their malice. God alone is author of all events; none may attribute to fortune.

Reformed hearing: light and darkness, well-being and calamity, are his; punishment-evil is his, guilt-evil is not; Pharaoh is used without inspired malice. Shared with Wesley: comforts and calamities from his hand; I am the LORD who does all these things. Historic sovereignty, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin comments KJV “peace and evil”; ESV is “well-being and calamity”—same lemma, not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast on 7: skip thin-versus-thick; both refuse fortune and both put calamity in his hand. Match v. 5–6: no other God. Match v. 8: the same LORD who created it.

verses.text: “Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it. Wesley: Drop—The righteous and gracious acts of God for his people, shall be so many, as if God rained showers of righteousness out of heaven. Open—Open itself to bring forth those fruits which may be expected from such showers. Them—The heavens and the earth conspiring together. Together—Together with salvation. It—This great work of salvation and righteousness; whereof, tho’ Cyrus is the instrument, I am the author.

Arminian hearing: showers of righteousness; earth opens to the fruit; heavens and earth conspire; Cyrus is the instrument, the LORD the author of this salvation and righteousness. Shared: Shower, O heavens; salvation and righteousness sprout; I the LORD have created it. Historic salvation via Cyrus, God the author—not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Drop” is his lemma for “Shower–rain down righteousness”; “It—Cyrus the instrument, I the author” names the same created work. Prefer no keyContrast on 8: Calvin’s Christ-kingdom is the larger end, not a millennial fork against Wesley’s instrument/author. Match v. 7: I the LORD who does all these things. Match v. 13: the same Cyrus stirred to build the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shower, O heavens, from above. Calvin: commands heaven and earth to bring forth salvation and righteousness. First: deliverance from Babylon, Cyrus the instrument. Then: these words bear a spiritual import to the kingdom of Christ, but first observe the simple interpretation about the return from captivity.

Reformed hearing: historic return first, Cyrus the instrument; Christ’s kingdom is the larger end, not a substitute for the captivity’s end. Shared with Wesley: Cyrus the instrument, the LORD the author; heavens and earth bring forth salvation and righteousness. Historic Babylon-return first, not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “bring forth salvation and righteousness” is his lemma for “salvation and righteousness may bear fruit.” Prefer no keyContrast on 8: both camps hear historic salvation via Cyrus with God as author; do not invent a millennial fork. Match v. 1: anointed Cyrus. Match v. 13: he shall build my city.

verses.text: “Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, ‘What are you making?’ or ‘Your work has no handles’?
verses.arminianNotes:
Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, What are you making? or Your work has no handles? Wesley: Woe—As God here makes many glorious promises to Cyrus, so he pronounces a curse upon them, who should endeavour to hinder him. Contend—Contend, if you please, with your fellow creatures, but not with your creator. Or—He turns his speech to the potter.

Arminian hearing: woe is a curse on those who would hinder Cyrus; contend with fellow creatures, not with your creator; the speech turns to the potter. Shared: woe to him who strives with his Maker; clay does not say to the potter, What are you making?; historic Maker. Historic woe around Cyrus’s commission, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Woe–hinder him” and “Contend–not with your creator” are his lemmas for “Woe to him who strives with him who formed him.” Match v. 1: glorious promises to the anointed Cyrus. Match v. 10: the same woe to him who questions father and mother. Match v. 13: him who must not be hindered, building the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Woe to him who strives with him who formed him. Calvin: restrains complaints of men who murmur in adversity and strive with God. Potsherd with potsherds; clay to the potter. Paul uses the same metaphor in Romans 9 for eternal predestination, but Calvin explicitly: Isaiah reasons about the course of the present life; Paul ascends to heavenly and eternal life. Do not treat Romans 9 as this verse’s subject.

Reformed hearing: woe restrains murmurers in adversity; clay has no right to debate the potter about the present life’s afflictions; Romans 9 is a higher subject, not Isaiah’s fight here. Shared with Wesley: woe to him who strives with his Maker; clay does not say to the potter, What are you making?; historic Maker. Historic Maker and present-life afflictions, not a newspaper, not a millennial or predestination camp fight imported from Paul. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “striveth with his Maker” is his lemma for “strives with him who formed him.” Match v. 7: the same LORD who creates calamity. Match v. 11: do not command him concerning his children.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings, with Wesley, take the Woe as a curse upon them who should endeavour to hinder Cyrus: contend, if you please, with your fellow creatures, but not with your creator; he turns his speech to the potter. Reformed readings, with Calvin, take the same Woe as restraining murmurers who in adversity strive with God: clay has no right to debate the potter about the present life’s afflictions; Paul’s Romans 9 use is a higher subject, not this verse’s fight. Shared: woe to him who strives with his Maker; clay does not say to the potter, What are you making?; historic Maker. Not a millennial camp fight, and not a predestination fork imported from Romans 9.

verses.text: Woe to him who says to a father, ‘What are you begetting?’ or to a woman, ‘With what are you in labor?’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? or to a woman, With what are you in labor? Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 9 honestly: Woe is a curse upon them who should endeavour to hinder Cyrus; contend with fellow creatures, not with your creator; he turns his speech to the potter. So here: Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? or to a woman, With what are you in labor?—the same strive-not-with-the-creator. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: questioning father and mother is the same woe as striving with the Maker who promised Cyrus. Shared: Woe to him who says to a father–; historic Maker. Historic family-and-potter figure, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast on 10: the real fork already sits on v. 9; do not duplicate it. Match v. 9: clay to the potter. Match v. 11: will you command me concerning my children.
verses.reformedNotes:
Woe to him who says to a father, What are you begetting? Calvin: grouped with v. 9—restrains murmurers who strive with God; potsherd with potsherds; clay to the potter. Isaiah reasons about the present life’s course, not Paul’s heavenly ascent.

Reformed hearing: questioning the begetting is the same murmur in adversity; the clay still has no right to debate. Shared with Wesley: Woe to him who says to a father–; historic Maker. Historic present-life figure, not a newspaper, not a Romans 9 import as this verse’s fight. Prefer no keyContrast on 10: the fork is v. 9’s hinder-Cyrus versus restrain-murmurers. Match v. 9: strives with him who formed him. Match v. 11: my children and the work of my hands.

verses.text: Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: “Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands?
verses.arminianNotes:
Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands? Wesley: Thus saith—Will you not allow me that liberty which yourselves take, of disposing of my own children and works, as I see fit?

Arminian hearing: he takes the same liberty they take—disposing of his own children and works as he sees fit; they may not command him. Shared: Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, the one who formed him; Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children. Historic Holy One of Israel, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Thus saith—liberty–disposing of my own children and works” is his lemma for “will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands.” No open theism: he already disposes as he sees fit. Prefer no keyContrast: both camps refuse prescribing to God. Match v. 9–10: clay and father. Match v. 12: I made the earth. Match v. 13: the work of his hands includes stirring Cyrus.
verses.reformedNotes:
Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him. Calvin: do not prescribe to God how to treat his sons and works. Ask of things to come is not a license to drag God to the bar.

Reformed hearing: inquiry about things to come is allowed; commanding him about his children is not; no bar for God. Shared with Wesley: he disposes of his own children and works; they may not command him. Historic Holy One who formed him, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “do not prescribe–sons and works” is his lemma for “will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands.” Prefer no keyContrast: both refuse the bar. Match v. 9: strive not with the Maker. Match v. 12–13: the Maker of earth stirs Cyrus.

verses.text: I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host.
verses.arminianNotes:
I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 11 honestly: Will you not allow me that liberty which yourselves take, of disposing of my own children and works, as I see fit? So here: I made the earth and created man on it; my hands stretched the heavens and commanded their host—the works he disposes. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: maker of earth, man, heavens, and host already has the liberty to dispose of children and works. Shared: I made the earth; created man; stretched out the heavens; commanded all their host. Historic Maker, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: skip rather than invent Wesley prose against Calvin’s sparrows. No open theism: he made and commanded; he is not learning the host. Match v. 11: the work of my hands. Match v. 13: the same hands make Cyrus’s ways level. Match 44:24: who alone stretched out the heavens.
verses.reformedNotes:
I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. Calvin: if he governs the world he cares for his family. Sparrows (Matt 10:29).

Reformed hearing: Maker of earth and heavens cares for his family as he cares for sparrows; government of the world is care, not absence. Shared with Wesley: I made the earth; created man; stretched the heavens; commanded the host. Historic Maker, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s sparrow-care (Matt 10:29) is his illustration of this making, not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast: Wesley has no extra lemma; skip rather than invent. Match v. 11: my children and the work of my hands. Match v. 13: I have stirred him up. Match 44:24: stretched out the heavens.

verses.text: I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward,” says the LORD of hosts.
verses.arminianNotes:
I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward, says the LORD of hosts. Wesley: Him—Cyrus. In righteousness—Most justly, to punish the wicked Babylonians, to plead the cause of the oppressed ones, to manifest my righteousness, and truth, and goodness.

Arminian hearing: him is Cyrus; righteousness is just punishment of Babylon, pleading the oppressed, manifesting righteousness, truth, and goodness; city built and exiles freed, not for price. Shared loudly: historic Persian Cyrus; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward. Historic Persian, not a newspaper, not a living politician, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Him—Cyrus” and “In righteousness—Most justly–” are his lemmas for “I have stirred him up in righteousness.” Prefer no keyContrast on 13: both camps take historic Cyrus building the city and releasing captives. No open theism: I have stirred him; I will make his ways level. Match v. 1: the same anointed Cyrus. Match 44:28: shepherd, Jerusalem built, temple foundation laid.
verses.reformedNotes:
I have stirred him up in righteousness. Calvin: faithfully, to manifest his righteousness in saving his people. Him is Cyrus. He shall build my city (by edicts, Ezra / 2 Chronicles) and release captives not for a price. Historic Persian, not a newspaper, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9.

Reformed hearing: raised in righteousness is faithful manifestation of righteousness in saving the people; city built by edicts; captives freed without price. Shared loudly with Wesley: Him is Cyrus; historic Persian king building the city and setting exiles free, not for price or reward. Historic Persian, not a living politician, not a millennial fork, not the Servant of 42:1–9. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “I have raised him up in righteousness” is his lemma for ESV “I have stirred him up in righteousness.” Prefer no keyContrast on 13: both camps share historic Cyrus. Match v. 1: his anointed, to Cyrus. Match 44:28: my shepherd; Jerusalem built; temple founded. Match v. 8: Cyrus the instrument, the LORD the author.
